clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of erythroderma, generalised lymphadenopathy, and clonal neoplastic T-cells (Sezary cells) in skin, lymph nodes, and peripheral blood
Regarded as the leukaemic and more aggressive counterpart of mycosis fungoides, though usually considered a distinct entity arising de novo
Patients typically have intense pruritus, scaling, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, ectropion, and alopecia, and are prone to skin infection
Sezary cells are mature CD4-positive memory T-cells with cerebriform nuclei, characteristically showing loss of pan-T-cell antigens such as CD7 and CD26
Diagnosis requires demonstrating a significant circulating clonal T-cell burden, for example by an elevated Sezary cell count or CD4-skewed ratio, matching the skin clone
Immune dysregulation increases susceptibility to infection, a major cause of death
Treatment favours skin-directed and immunomodulatory approaches such as extracorporeal photopheresis, retinoids, and interferon, escalating to systemic therapy as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Sezary syndrome is a leukaemic form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in which malignant mature CD4-positive memory T-cells with characteristic cerebriform (Sezary) nuclei circulate in the blood and infiltrate the skin and lymph nodes. Loss of normal T-cell surface antigens and skin-homing receptor expression allows widespread cutaneous seeding, producing erythroderma. The expanding neoplastic clone disrupts normal T-cell function and cytokine balance, causing profound pruritus and immune dysregulation that predisposes to recurrent infection. Progressive disease can transform to large-cell morphology with a more aggressive behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Benign (reactive) erythroderma from eczema, psoriasis, or drug reaction
Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma with skin involvement
Actinic reticuloid and other pseudolymphomatous conditions
Other peripheral T-cell lymphomas with erythroderma
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry for T-cell markers
Peripheral blood flow cytometry for CD4/CD8 ratio and loss of CD7 and CD26
Sezary cell count and quantification of the circulating clonal burden
Matched T-cell receptor clonality studies on blood and skin
Lymph node evaluation and cross-sectional imaging for staging
Assessment for infection and monitoring of the skin barrier
redFlags: Sepsis arising from a compromised, erythrodermic skin barrier
Large-cell transformation with rapidly enlarging tumours
Severe metabolic disturbance from extensive skin failure (fluid loss, thermoregulatory compromise)
reference.prognosis: Sezary syndrome is generally aggressive with a guarded long-term outlook; disease burden, large-cell transformation, and infective complications drive mortality, though immunomodulatory therapy can provide meaningful disease control.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic erythroderma to benign dermatitis and missing the underlying lymphoma
Failing to demonstrate a matched circulating clone required for diagnosis
Underestimating infection risk from the failing skin barrier
Not recognising large-cell transformation that changes prognosis and treatment
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Refer all confirmed or suspected cases to a specialized cutaneous lymphoma or hemato-oncology center given the complexity of staging and treatment options.

Base treatment intensity on stage and extent of skin, blood, nodal, and visceral involvement rather than a single fixed protocol; most patients need systemic and immunomodulatory therapy given the circulating clonal burden inherent to Sezary syndrome.
Use skin-directed measures such as topical corticosteroids for symptom control, and total-skin electron beam therapy for erythrodermic disease or palliation.

Consider extracorporeal photopheresis as a mainstay for patients with significant blood involvement, often combined with bexarotene and or interferon-alfa, and consider combining photopheresis with total-skin electron beam therapy for improved outcomes in erythrodermic patients.

Consider systemic agents including interferon-alfa, oral bexarotene (monitoring for lipid elevation and thyroid suppression), mogamulizumab (an anti-CCR4 antibody preferred specifically for Sezary syndrome given strong clearance of circulating leukemic cells), histone deacetylase inhibitors, and brentuximab vedotin when CD30 expression is present.
Reserve denileukin diftitox and alemtuzumab for relapsed or refractory disease when better-tolerated antibody-based options are not suitable.

Prefer single-agent cytotoxic chemotherapy over multi-agent regimens for advanced refractory disease, reserving combination chemotherapy for extensive adenopathy, visceral involvement, or need for rapid disease control.

Evaluate transplant-eligible patients, particularly younger patients with aggressive relapsed or refractory disease, for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only approach reported to offer durable, potentially curative control.
Monitor serially with skin disease assessment, circulating Sezary cell counts, and imaging at initial staging and follow-up for nodal or visceral progression, with biopsy of enlarged nodes.

Perform bone marrow assessment in advanced disease or when hematologic function is compromised, and watch closely for large-cell transformation and infection given profound immunosuppression and skin-barrier compromise.
Refer promptly for infection management, since immunosuppression and skin-barrier failure are major drivers of morbidity and mortality.
